title: Jansenism
hookLine: a strict movement kept people from communion; the Church later encouraged frequent communion

cards: "Lord, I am not worthy." Just before communion at Mass, Catholics say a line borrowed from a centurion, an army officer, in the Gospel of Matthew.
In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed." Two halves.
Now suppose someone took the first half so seriously they never reached the second. Suppose they decided the table was for people who had earned it, and stayed in the pew, waiting to be good enough.
Today, a movement that pulled people that way.

teach.b: First, a book. Cornelius Jansen, a bishop in Flanders, spent years studying Saint Augustine on grace. His long book on Augustine came out after his death, and the movement that followed took his name: Jansenism.
It painted fallen human nature in very dark colors and was severe about who could be saved. Popes later condemned propositions drawn from the book. Second, a convent.

The Cistercian nuns of Port-Royal, near Paris, became the movement's heart. Antoine Arnauld, a theologian close to them, wrote a book on frequent communion urging long preparation and real penance before receiving.
The philosopher Blaise Pascal took their side in a public quarrel. These were serious, prayerful people who wanted reverence. Third, the cost.

In practice, communion started to look like a reward for the nearly perfect. Some Catholics went a long time without receiving, afraid they would never be worthy. Fear of sin began to crowd out trust in mercy.
Fourth, the Church's answer. Over time, Rome pushed the other way. Pope Pius X urged Catholics to receive often, even daily, and opened communion to young children.
Pope Francis has written that the Eucharist is not a prize for the perfect but medicine and food for the weak. The Church still asks anyone aware of grave sin to go to confession first.
That isn't Jansenism; it's a door, not a wall.

teach.h: THEY THAT ARE IN HEALTH NEED NOT A PHYSICIAN.
teach.b: Jesus said it plainly in Matthew: "They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill."

how: Catholics who are free of grave sin are encouraged to receive communion often, even daily, and before receiving they say together a form of the centurion's words from Matthew 8:8, confessing they are not worthy and asking only for a word of healing.

o: a strict movement that made communion feel earned
a reform that urged daily communion for all
a school that said grace wasn't needed at all

p: a bishop who wrote on Augustine and grace
the convent at the movement's heart

s: the Church sided with the Jansenists on communion
popes condemned propositions drawn from Jansen's book, and later urged Catholics to receive often.
the words 'Lord, I am not worthy' come from a centurion in Matthew
the centurion asks Jesus to heal his servant: only say the word.
receiving often means confession no longer matters
the Church still asks anyone aware of grave sin to go to confession first. a door, not a wall.

games.q: you're a Catholic who has been to confession, but you still feel you're not good enough. Sunday comes. what do you do?
o: stay in the pew until you feel perfect.
receive, trusting it's food for the weak.
stop going to Mass at all.
games.why: the Church's answer, against the Jansenist mood, is to receive. the Mass even has you say 'I am not worthy' right before you do.

practice: If you receive communion, think of the next time you will, and answer any voice that says you haven't earned it with the whole of the centurion's line, both halves.
If you don't, bring to mind one gift you felt you didn't deserve, a kindness, a second chance, a meal, and hold it like a gift, not a debt. Let it stay unearned.

wordCard.voice: Jansenism. A strict movement named for Bishop Cornelius Jansen, severe about grace and wary of frequent communion, which the Church came to resist.

orig.note: Latin: Lord, I am not worthy, the centurion's words from Matthew 8:8, said before communion.

carryVoice: Your line: not a reward. The week ran from honest martyrs and a gentle bishop to organized charity, sisters on the street, a heart on fire and an open table. Another week, done.

sources.q: Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed.
They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill.
